title: The thread that won't break
hook: such a thread doesn't break, burn, get dirty or wear out (Asa di Var, ang 471)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janeu: compassion the cotton, the thread of the soul. Today, the second half of that salok, and four things that thread can survive.

Open any drawer at home and you'll find something that wore out. A sweater with elbows gone thin. A phone cable split near the plug. A favorite shirt washed one too many times. Everything made of fiber frays eventually. Cotton breaks under strain. It burns in a second near a flame. It picks up stains. And even protected from all that, time thins it out. Guru Nanak named all four ways a thread can fail, one by one, about the thread of compassion from yesterday.
screen: `A SWEATER WITH THIN ELBOWS.` → `EVERY FIBER FRAYS.` → `FOUR WAYS A THREAD FAILS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the salok on ang 471 continues, in paraphrase. Such a thread doesn't break. It doesn't get dirty. It doesn't burn. It isn't lost. Blessed, Nanak says, are the people who go about wearing it around their necks. Four nots. One way to hear them: breaking is strain, the hard week, the argument, the shock. Dirt is the slow grime of daily life: resentment, envy, gossip. Burning is the sudden fire: rage, disaster, loss. And being lost is time itself, the way things simply slip away. A cotton thread can't survive any of these for long. A thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth, the salok says, survives all four. Then Guru Nanak looks at the outer thread with plain eyes. It's bought for a few coins, he says, and put on in a ceremony. When the body dies, it falls away; the person leaves without it. Whatever is tied to the body goes the way of the body. The next salok in the var adds an answer. Through trust in the Name, honor arises, and praise of the One is the true thread. Worn that way, it doesn't break in the Court of the Lord. Sikh teaching reads this as a question about what goes with us. Not possessions, not status, not even the symbols we're given. What goes is what we've become. A grandmother who has worn that thread for decades, patient at the stove, honest at the market, takes it with her. The cotton one stays behind.
screen: `IT WON'T BREAK, STAIN, BURN, OR BE LOST.` · `THE OUTER THREAD FALLS AWAY.` · `PRAISE IS THE TRUE THREAD.` · `WHAT GOES IS WHAT WE'VE BECOME.` · then, large: `IT WON'T WEAR OUT.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself many years from now, most of today's worries long gone, and ask what in you will still be there: not a job title, maybe a way of listening, a patience, a love for certain people. Let one quality come forward, and picture it as a thread, already strong, getting stronger. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Compassion, one strand of the soul's thread: in Guru Nanak's salok, spun with contentment, restraint and truth, it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost, and it goes with you.
Your line: it won't wear out. What goes with us is what we've become. Five hundred fifty-five days now.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that virtues and the praise of the One are what go with a person beyond death.

chat.says: If the cotton thread falls away at death, what thread goes with a person?
options: What we've become: a thread of compassion, contentment, restraint and truth doesn't break or burn.
The cotton one, if kept clean and whole: the salok says a well-kept thread never falls away.
The thread bought for coins: the salok says the outer one stays, and the inner one fades.
chat.meaning: The outer thread falls away with the body, the salok says. The soul's thread doesn't break, get dirty, burn or get lost.
